page_title: Dress Up's Hardest Parts for Hazel
title: Dress Up in Hazel: the hard part of the drawing is what runs every frame, the music can be computed, and the menus need a layout Hazel lacks
sub: Matthew asked three questions about porting Messed Up Dress Up to Hazel (ticket 402): which parts of the drawing would be hardest for Hazel, whether Hazel can do music, and how to offer the game's menus in Hazel while keeping to Always Be Knolling. He also asked for the game's advanced features, staged as challenges. It builds on ^du_report(8) (the port, piece by piece), ^du_report(5) (the menu rules) and ^report(15) (the game and its livelits, measured side by side). The game at 0.0.334; Hazel on its livelits × modular editors branch (hazelgrove/hazel#2635) at 90ed4505bf.
answers: The drawing's hard part is not its SVG but what runs around it. A Hazel view can draw every element the game uses (41 SVG element kinds, gradients, clips, masks, filters and animations included). What Hazel lacks is what the game does at run time: motion every frame (a livelit has no clock, and a change costs 0.13 to 1.09 s against a frame's 16.7 ms), measuring the drawn picture (about 100 calls place things on it), its sizes (the greenhouse has 1,906 elements; the largest Hazel picture so far, 570 shapes), and byte-exact numbers: Hazel's to_fixed and the game's f1 disagree on 5 of 7 values tried.

Music: Hazel can compute it today; playing it takes a JS player or a new builtin. 63% of the game's music code is pure (the tunes, chords, arrangements and the score of note events). A Hazel program computed a 1,216-event score, the size of the forest tune's, in about 0.2 s. A livelit cannot make a sound; Hazel's MVU apps can, a sine beep (Cmd.PlayTone) with timers, which corrects ^du_report(8)'s "no sound binding".

The menus: Hazel meets about two of the nine knolling rules, and the gap is a layout, then speed. Livelits show up inline, stacked in the UX outline, or in a sidebar column; none is a grid of named boxes. The plan: the settings as a tree of modules, a "knolled" UX layout that draws modules as tabs and their members as boxes, and big livelits for the bespoke designers. Even laid out right, each change costs 0.13 to 1.2 s; the rule "keep it fast" waits on Hazel's speed.

The advanced features fall into six stages, from pictures Hazel can draw today, through small builtins, a clock for livelits, interaction inside the picture and the designers, to the whole game at 60 fps, which waits until a change costs about 16 ms.

drawing.intro: What the game's drawing uses (counted in js/, 0.0.334) and what it rests on at run time:
runtime: Measuring the drawn picture (getBBox, getScreenCTM, getBoundingClientRect, getPointAtLength)
about 104 calls: collision boxes, where tree-room pictures hang, ladders, foam layers, a lifted thing's centre
walking, climbing, treading water, bubbles and balls, the leak, blowing
poses' phases, and 43 places that time scenery to the music
the depth sort, the friend put in front of what is behind their feet, reusing unchanged pieces, still pictures on slow computers
a sine hash, Math.sin(seed·71.3 + i·13.7)·43758.5453, in 467 calls
hardest: Livelits have no clock, and a change costs 0.13 to 1.09 s, against 16.7 ms a frame.
Hazel computes the poses at sampled phases and writes the animation as SMIL or CSS; JS keeps the frame loop and the simulations.
There is no way to measure layout from Hazel; about 104 calls rely on it.
A bounds library in Hazel (boxes from the geometry, with transforms and curves), or a measuring command for views.
The imagination is 2.45 MB; the greenhouse 1,906 elements; Hazel's largest picture so far is 570 shapes.
Static scenery as one picture (an <img> from a Hazel string), only the friend as structured elements; memos keyed by explicit inputs.
The depth sort, the friend's place, piece reuse and still pictures happen after drawing.
The sort and the friend's place in Hazel (they are pure over name, depth and SVG); stills and bitmaps stay in JS.
f1 is used 7,269 times and differs from to_fixed (below); the sine hash multiplies any 1-ulp difference by 43,758.
An f1-like number-to-text builtin, and a check that sin agrees bit for bit.
drawing.try_note: The game's f1 is (Math.round(x · 10) / 10).toString(): it rounds halves up and drops a trailing .0; Hazel's to_fixed(x, 1) keeps the .0 and rounds the binary value. Run with Hazel's command-line tool (013/data/numbers.hz) and the game's f1 in node.

split: notation and part builders, the 45 tunes and their arrangements, the score (songOf: a sorted list of events, each with a start, length, notes, part and velocity), timing, the LFOs, the mix's maths
34 synthesizer instruments in WebAudio, effects and reverb, a scheduler that sends notes 0.5 s ahead on the audio clock, the mixing board, the transport

music.try_note: A tune as data, one bar of (note, length) pairs repeated for a form, turned into (start, note, length) events by a recursive Hazel function (013/data/score.hz). Wall time of Hazel's command-line tool on the Ubuntu laptop (Intel i7), three runs each; the work is the difference from the start-up-only run.

rules: A box for each thing you can see or hear, named once
Misses: a UX cell is headed by the binding's name, the Projectors card by printed syntax
Misses in the UX outline (a flat stack); nested livelits could do it
Knolled: a grid, things of a kind the same size
Misses: a stack or a column
Partly: one binding, but a box cannot be shown in two places
Partly: the picture can be a UX cell, not a sticky first card
Misses: a change costs 0.13 s (Kids' Choice) to 1.2 s (Full Body in the UX outline), against Dress Up's 1.4 ms
options: One big livelit whose view is the menu

Full control of tabs, grids and pictures; but its open tab and folds live in its model, so every click is an edit (and an undo step) costing about a second; good for bounded designers (the world grid, the castle map, the mixer)
A knolled UX layout
Modules as tabs, their members as boxes in a grid, the picture as a sticky first card, tab and fold state kept by the editor, not in the program: meets rules 1, 2, 3 and 8, partly 7
The program organized as the menu
A module per tab and a submodule per box, each setting a livelit; works with today's UX outline, but only as a flat stack
An MVU app in the sidebar
Fast, but its state is not program text, so the program cannot read the settings: rewriting the game as an app
menus.plan: The program organized as the menu, with a knolled UX layout over it, and big livelits for the bespoke designers: as the game itself has generic boxes for most tabs and its own full screens for music, the world and the castle.

next: Port the face alone (431 lines) and time it, as ^du_report(8) proposed; add an f1-like builtin first, so the picture can be compared byte for byte.
Port the forest tune's score: compare its events one by one with the game's songOf("forest"), then play them through the game's own instruments from JSON.
Try a view with an <audio> of the archive's recording, the cheapest sound in Hazel today.
Prototype the knolled UX layout on one tab (the friend's face): modules as boxes, the picture as the first card.
Ask the Hazel team about a clock (a subscription) for livelits: it unlocks stage 3 and most of stage 4.
method: Three read-only passes over the code on 2026-10-19: the game's drawing, its music and its menus (js/ at 0.0.334, the picture archive of 0.0.304, ^du_report(5) and (8)), and Hazel's livelits branch (hazelgrove/hazel#2635) for what a view can draw, what a livelit can do, and where livelits show up. Counts are of lines in js/; sizes are from the archive.

Two tries, run with Hazel's command-line tool (its run command) on #2635 at 90ed4505bf, on the Ubuntu laptop (Intel i7): the number formatting (013/data/numbers.hz) and the score (013/data/score.hz, score760.hz), three runs each for the timings.
Hazel's speed figures (0.13 to 1.09 s a change, 570 shapes) are from ^report(15) and the Hazel reports, not measured again here.
